name: Klaverjassen
description: Klaverjassen (also spelled Klaverjas) is one of the most popular card games in the Netherlands, traditionally played in cafes, social clubs, and at home. It is a trick-taking game for four players in partnerships, characterized by its unique trump ranking (where Jack and Nine are the highest cards) and the scoring of 'roem' (bonus points for card combinations). The game has several regional variants named after Dutch cities: Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Utrecht.

overview.description: Klaverjassen (also spelled Klaverjas) is one of the most popular card games in the Netherlands, traditionally played in cafes, social clubs, and at home. It is a trick-taking game for four players in partnerships, characterized by its unique trump ranking (where Jack and Nine are the highest cards) and the scoring of 'roem' (bonus points for card combinations). The game has several regional variants named after Dutch cities: Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Utrecht.

history.origins: Klaverjassen developed from the Jass family of games that originated in the Low Countries. The name comes from 'Klaverjas' (Jack of Clubs), reflecting the importance of the Jack in trump. The game became the dominant card game in the Netherlands during the 19th and 20th centuries.
timeline: 1800s: Jass games spread through the Netherlands and Belgium
Late 1800s: Klaverjassen establishes itself as the Dutch national card game
1900s: Regional variants develop in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Utrecht
Present: Remains extremely popular in Dutch cafes and social clubs; played in organized competitions
history.cultural: Klaverjassen is deeply embedded in Dutch cafÃ© culture. It is one of the few games where signaling conventions (within strict rules) are an accepted part of play. The game is often played in social clubs and at family gatherings.
history.evolution: The game evolved distinct Dutch characteristics including the 'roem' (melds) system and specific trump-choosing conventions. The Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Utrecht variants differ mainly in rules about when trumps must be played.

setup.players: 4 players in partnerships, partners sitting opposite each other.
setup.deck: 32-card Piquet deck: 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, King, Ace in each suit. Dutch cards often use A (Aas), H (Heer), V (Vrouw), B (Boer) for indices.
setup.dealing: Deal in three groups: first 3 cards each, then 2 cards each, then 3 cards each. Alternatively, deal in two groups of 4 cards each.

rules.objective: Score as many points as possible over 16 hands. In each hand, the team that chooses trumps must collect more than half the available points (81+ out of 162). If they fail, the opposing team gets all the points.
rules.gameplay: Player to dealer's left leads to first trick. Must follow suit if possible. Amsterdam rules: If cannot follow and opponent is winning, must beat with trump if possible. If partner is winning, may play any card (except cannot undertrump). Rotterdam rules: Must always play trump if cannot follow suit; must beat any trumps already played if possible.
keyRules: Trump ranking: Jack (20), Nine (14), Ace (11), Ten (10), King (4), Queen (3), Eight (0), Seven (0)
Plain suit ranking: Ace (11), Ten (10), King (4), Queen (3), Jack (2), Nine (0), Eight (0), Seven (0)
Must follow suit, must trump if cannot follow (Rotterdam)
Roem (melds): sequences and four-of-a-kinds score bonus points

strategy.basic: The Jack and Nine of trumps are the most powerful cards (34 points together). If you have these, you have strong control of the trump suit. Always try to establish how many trumps your partner holds.
strategy.intermediate: Roem (melds) can significantly affect the score. A run of 3 (20 points) or 4 (50 points) can swing a hand. Be careful not to give opponents the cards they need for their melds. The Stuk (trump King and Queen) is worth 20 points and should be protected.
strategy.advanced: Signaling: Partners use legal signals to communicate hand strength. A high-low signal in a suit suggests an even number of cards; low-high suggests odd. Master the Amsterdam vs Rotterdam rules about when you must trumpâ€”this affects endgame play significantly.
tips: Remember the two different card orders: trick-taking order (Jack, Nine high in trumps) vs meld sequence order (Ace high)
The last trick is worth 10 pointsâ€”plan accordingly
If you choose trumps, you need 82+ points to score; aim for at least 90 to be safe
Four Jacks is worth 200 pointsâ€”nearly enough to win a hand by itself
In Amsterdam rules, you can 'throw off' when partner is winning; in Rotterdam, you must always trump if possible
